title: 200 core words

segments.voice: Yesterday, 200 core words and atman: the self lifting the self, its own friend or its own enemy. Today, one word that two schools read two ways.

A magician saws an assistant in half, and the room splits too: some people want the trick explained, and some would rather keep the wonder. Sanskrit has a word that sits right on that line. In the Gita's seventh chapter, Krishna calls it mama maya, my maya, and says it's hard to cross. Illusion, or God's real power? Two classic teachers answer differently, and each answer is worth hearing at its best.
screen: `EXPLAIN THE TRICK, OR KEEP THE WONDER?` → `MAMA MAYA: MY MAYA.` → `ILLUSION, OR POWER?`

segments.voice: First the verse: daivi hy esha gunamayi mama maya duratyaya. This divine maya of mine, made of the gunas, is hard to cross. Then: mam eva ye prapadyante mayam etam taranti te. Those who come to me alone cross over this maya. Both readers keep every word. Both agree the maya is Krishna's own, and both agree it can be crossed. They read maya itself differently. In Advaita, the school linked with the teacher Shankara, there is one reality, Brahman, and maya is how that one appears as many. The world isn't nothing. It's real enough to live in, the way a dream is real while it lasts. But it isn't the final truth, and crossing maya means waking to the one. In Vishishtadvaita, the school linked with Ramanuja, maya in this verse is God's own wondrous power, the stuff of the world he works through. The world is real, and it belongs to God the way a body belongs to a self. Crossing maya means not being caught by it, by turning to the one who wields it. Each side, at its strongest. Advaita: if there is truly one, the many must be a kind of appearance. Ramanuja: if God shapes the world and calls the power his own, calling it unreal sells the work short. The verse says mama, mine, and leaves the rest to its readers. For a reader of Sanskrit, that is the lesson of some core words: knowing what maya can mean is the start, and knowing who reads it how is the rest.
screen: `MAMA MAYA, HARD TO CROSS.` · `ADVAITA: THE ONE APPEARING AS MANY.` · `RAMANUJA: GOD'S REAL POWER.` · `EACH SIDE, AT ITS STRONGEST.` · then, large: `ONE VERSE, TWO READINGS.`

segments.voice: Pick one object near you, a cup, a leaf, your own hand, and look at it for the sit. For a while, see it as Advaita might: a form the one reality is wearing. Then as Ramanuja might: something real, shaped and held. Don't choose; just look.
Two hundred core words: today, maya, and mama, mine. One verse, two classic readings: the one appearing as many, or God's own wondrous power.

fork.setup: your friend loves Ramanuja's reading and asks you to give Advaita's best case in one line. which do you send?
options: 'if there's truly one reality, the many must be how it appears.'
'the world is fake, so nothing you do matters.'
'maya is God's real power, and the world is his.'
fork.reveal: that's Advaita at its strongest: one reality, appearing as many. the second is a caricature; the third is Ramanuja's own view.

chat.says: cousin says the whole fight between dad and uncle vikram is 'just maya' so why bother. is that the gita?
options: one school calls the world appearance but livable; another calls it God's real work. neither says "don't bother."
yes: every Hindu school agrees maya means nothing is real, so family fights don't matter.
no: in the Gita maya only means a stage magician's trick; it has nothing to do with the world.
chat.meaning: Advaita reads maya as the one appearing as many; Ramanuja reads it as God's real power. Neither reading calls ordinary life pointless.
